title: How the Brain Processes Information to Make Decisions - Reflective and Reactive Systems

segments.title: Reflective and Reactive Decision Systems
segments.script: Picture two taxi drivers on the same route. One has driven this exact taxi rank to town road for fifteen years. When a pothole suddenly appears, or a car cuts in from a side street, he swerves and brakes without even thinking about it. His hands and feet just know what to do. That is your brain's reactive system at work: quick, intuitive, driven by habit and emotion, and controlled by older, more primitive parts of the brain, the basal ganglia and amygdala. Now picture that same driver sitting down at the end of the month trying to decide whether to buy a new taxi engine or fix the old one. He pulls out his notebook, checks the fuel costs, asks his mechanic, compares prices, and thinks it through carefully. That is the reflective system: logical, analytical, slow, and deliberate, run mainly by the prefrontal cortex, the part of the brain behind your forehead. Here is the important part. Scientists tell us the brain can only use one of these systems at a time, not both together. And neither system is automatically better than the other, it depends on the situation. If a shopkeeper at a spaza shop sees someone reaching under the counter suspiciously, she does not sit down and weigh pros and cons, she reacts instantly, and that reaction could save her life. Experienced managers, like a taxi association chairperson who has settled route disputes for years, often make fast decisions that feel like gut instinct, but really that gut feeling is built from years of pattern recognition. On the other hand, big, unfamiliar decisions, like whether to expand a stokvel into a formal investment club, need the slow, careful reflective route, not a rushed one. The tricky part is emotion. Strong feelings, whether excitement or anger, pull us toward the fast reactive system even when the decision deserves careful thought. Think about buying something on impulse at Shoprite because it was on special, then regretting it when you check your bank balance. That is emotion hijacking your decision-making. Good managers do not ignore emotions though, because emotions carry useful signals, especially about right and wrong. The skill of noticing, understanding, and managing your own emotions and other people's emotions is called emotional intelligence. A manager with strong emotional intelligence at a Joburg clinic, for example, can sense when a team is stressed after a difficult shift and knows to pause before making a big staffing decision, rather than reacting in frustration. Emotional intelligence blends self-awareness, self-control, empathy for others, and social skill in managing relationships. It is not something you either have or do not have, it is a muscle you build with practice, and it helps you know when to trust your gut and when to slow down and think things through properly.
keyPoints: The brain uses two decision systems, reflective and reactive, and only one operates at a time
The reactive system is fast and intuitive, useful for danger or for experienced experts, but risky for big novel decisions
The reflective system is slow, logical and better for important or unfamiliar decisions
Emotional intelligence means managing your own and others' emotions so you know when to react and when to reflect
segments.altExplanation: Think of your brain like a taxi that has two gears, a fast gear and a slow gear. The fast gear, the reactive system, lets you swerve around a pothole without thinking, using instinct built from experience. The slow gear, the reflective system, is for navigating unfamiliar roads with a map, checking each turn carefully. You cannot drive in both gears at once. A skilled driver knows which gear the road demands. Similarly, a skilled manager knows when a decision needs instant reaction, like handling a sudden complaint from an angry customer, and when it needs the slow gear, like deciding whether to close a branch. Choosing the wrong gear, rushing a big decision or overthinking an emergency, causes problems.
segments.deeper: Neuropsychology research, including work by Darlow and Sloman, shows these two systems are not just metaphors but are tied to distinct brain regions, with the prefrontal cortex handling reflective processing and the basal ganglia and amygdala handling reactive processing. This matters for managers because it explains why stress and time pressure change decision quality. Under intense pressure, the brain naturally shifts toward the reactive system, even for decisions that deserve careful analysis, which is why organizations build in cooling off periods before major decisions, such as retrenchments or large purchases. It also explains why expertise matters so much in fast paced roles. What looks like lucky instinct in an experienced manager is often compressed reflective thinking from past situations, now running on autopilot. The danger is when reactive shortcuts are applied to genuinely novel problems, since patterns from the past may not fit. This is why emotional intelligence sits alongside the two systems in the chapter, because managing emotional arousal is often the deciding factor in which system takes control of a given decision.
segments.example: A branch manager at a bank in Durban gets a furious call from a client whose card was blocked. Her first impulse is to snap back defensively, a reactive response fuelled by irritation. Recognising this, she takes a breath, waits a moment, and reflectively considers the client's history and the bank's policy before responding calmly with a solution. By managing her emotional reaction and switching to the reflective system, she resolves the complaint professionally instead of escalating it.

checkpoint.prompt: Explain the two systems used by the brain in decision-making.
checkpoint.answer: The brain processes information to make decisions using one of two systems: either the logical, rational (reflective) system or the quick, reactive system. The reflective system is better for significant and important decisions; these generally should not be rushed. However, the reactive system can be lifesaving when time is of the essence, and it can be much more efficient when based on developed experience and expertise.
checkpoint.rubric: Answer must name both systems (reflective and reactive), describe reflective as logical/analytical/methodical and better for important decisions, and describe reactive as quick/intuitive and useful in urgent situations or when based on experience/expertise.

checkpoint.prompt: What is emotional intelligence, and why is it important for decision-making?
checkpoint.answer: Emotional intelligence is the ability to recognize, understand, pay attention to, and manage one's own emotions and the emotions of others. It involves self-awareness, self-regulation, empathy, and social skills. It is important because effective decision-making relies on both logic and emotions, and managers who understand their own and others' emotions can use that awareness to guide better individual and group decision-making.
checkpoint.rubric: Answer must define emotional intelligence as recognizing and managing one's own and others' emotions, mention at least two of self-awareness, self-regulation, empathy, or social skills, and explain its importance as helping managers make better decisions or manage group decision-making.

checkpoint.prompt: Which part of the brain is more involved in the reactive decision-making system?
checkpoint.rubric: Correct answer is basal ganglia and amygdala, matching the text's description of the reactive system's brain regions.

checkpoint.prompt: Why might a manager choose to delay a decision until after strong emotions have settled?
checkpoint.answer: Because intense emotions, positive or negative, pull decision-makers toward the fast reactive system, which can lead to impulsive choices; waiting allows the reflective system to take over for a more logical, well-considered decision.
checkpoint.rubric: Answer must state that strong emotions push people toward reactive/impulsive decisions and that waiting allows more logical or reflective processing before deciding.
